Issued at 129 AM MDT Wed Jul 29 2026

Sometimes when forecasting the weather, you feel like you are 
trapped in a time warp, with the same concerns day after day. For 
much of may last string of shifts, the concern was the monsoon and 
hot temperatures. And as I arrive back on shift tonight, the concern 
once again is the monsoon and hot temperatures. However, one will be 
of somewhat less concern than last week.

And that one thing will be the monsoon. We will have another surge 
of monsoonal moisture moving northward across the area today with a 
shortwave crossing the area. Radar shows some showers moving 
toward the southern border, and these will move northward 
through the day. Precipitable water values are rather high 
today, over an inch in some locations. This would put portions 
of the area over 150 percent of normal (average this time of 
year is around 0.60 inches). However, it is less than the 200 to
250 percent of last week. Steering flow is not the strongest 
though. A few parts of the area are under a marginal risk of 
excessive rainfall, mainly far southern and eastern portions of 
the area. So there is some risk of local flooding, but the risk 
looks low. Most convection should end after sunset, although a 
few showers may linger after midnight. As for temperatures, with
more cloud cover spreading over the area, temperatures should 
be cooler than yesterday. We did lower temperatures a few 
degrees, with many locations staying in the 80s for highs today,
mainly in the southern half of the County Warning Area.

Then, starting on Thursday, we will begin to move into what is known 
as an inverse relationship, where one thing goes up and another goes 
down. And in this case, temperatures will be the thing on the way 
up, and the chance of convection as well as humidity will be on the 
way down. On Thursday, precipitable water values drop around 20 to 
30 percent across the area. They will still be somewhat above normal 
but only about 120 percent of normal versus over 150 percent. There 
will still be some convection around but less then Wednesday, with 
most concentrated in and near the mountains. But even here, the 
chance is generally 1 out of 3 or less. Temperatures will also begin 
to rise again, to generally about 5 degrees above normal which would 
put highs in the 90s across most locations below 5500 feet once 
again. Precipitable water values continue to drop on Friday as the 
core of the moisture continues to get pushed to the east. Any storms 
on this day would likely be restricted to the eastern portions
of the County Warning Area. Temperatures should run similar to 
Thursday, very warm but not unusual for the latter part of July.

The main concern then shifts to heat, possibly record breaking heat, 
for the first weekend of August. Another heat dome will continue to 
build northward, bringing 500 millibar heights as high as 5980 
meters and 700 millibar temperatures as high as 23 degrees celsius. 
This will lead to another very hot weekend. Saturday looks hot, with 
at least a 1 in 2 chance of high temperatures of 100 or greater 
across elevations under 5500 feet. However, the warmest day 
looks to Sunday, when a tightening pressure gradient ahead of an
advancing cold front will bring a gusty, southwesterly 
downsloping breeze. At this time, there is at least a 9 in 10 
chance of high temperatures over 100 in locations under 5500 
feet, with around an 1 in 2 chance of temperatures 105 or warmer
below 4800 feet. Some locations have already set new monthly 
record highs 3 times this year (March, May and July); and this 
could occur again for August. For example, it has never been 100
degrees at the Riverton airport in August, and it is highly 
likely this will occur on Sunday afternoon. And, this will raise
another concern, possible critical fire weather. Humidity will 
be very low on this day, with most areas East of the Divide 
seeing humidity in the single digits. With the gusty wind, we 
may need some fire weather highlights for Sunday afternoon as 
the front approaches. In addition, this looks like a dry frontal
passage with any convection likely remaining over Montana.

We may finally have some relief from the heat on Monday after the 
frontal passage, especially East of the Divide. The 700 millibar 
temperatures fall as much as 6 to 7 degrees celsius, which could 
drop temperatures back into the 80s for most locations. The 
front may be slow to move West of the Divide so there could be 
one more very warm day there before cooler air moves in for 
Tuesday. The concern for fire weather may continue here is as 
well, with humidity remaining low and a gusty breeze continuing.
Ridging may then begin building northward again, bringing more 
above normals temperatures for the latter half of next week.
